A waived bank fee has an opportunity cost: compare the extra balance and the saved cash

Four interactive graphics compare equal starting funds and monthly budgets, reconcile saved fees with forgone interest and test fewer qualifying months.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare a retained balance with the same funds earning an assumed yield

Interactive planning lab

Ending resources · A minus B$236.93
Fees avoided and actually saved, before growth$960
Break-even additional balance under these assumptions$6,487.53

Original hypothetical CAD comparison with equal initial extra funds and the same outside monthly budget. A retains the additional balance in non-interest chequing; in qualifying months, its unused fee budget is saved at month-end in a separate account earning the assumed net yield. Otherwise that budget pays the fee. B puts the same initial funds in the alternative account; the same outside monthly budget pays every fee. B fees are not also deducted from its investment balance. Common operating cash and all other household flows are excluded equally. Only the first selected number of months in each repeated year qualify; eligibility is independently assumed, never inferred from a monthly average or from the additional balance. No daily account ledger or actual bank threshold is calculated. The alternative yield is a constant effective annual net assumption converted to an equivalent monthly rate, not a quoted or guaranteed return. No separate tax, fee change, inflation, account-access feature or product recommendation is calculated.

On this page

  1. Confirm the waiver condition before comparing the dollars
  2. Give both alternatives the same starting money and outside budget
  3. Reconcile the ending resources instead of treating the waived fee as a yield

The central idea

Compare the additional balance needed for a waiver with the alternative use of that same money. Count waived fees as additional resources only when the freed budget is actually retained.

01

Confirm the waiver condition before comparing the dollars

A monthly account fee is visible on a statement. The alternative use of money kept in the account is less visible, but it still belongs in a financial plan.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s chequing-account guidance explains that some accounts waive a monthly fee when a minimum balance is maintained. It also warns that a balance dipping below the requirement for even one day can result in the fee being charged.

Check the actual agreement’s measurement rule, qualifying dates and included services. A monthly average is not a substitute for a required daily minimum. This tool accepts a qualifying-month pattern supplied separately; it does not determine whether the entered extra balance satisfies a particular bank’s terms.

Use the additional money needed solely for the waiver. Operating cash that would remain in the account under either approach belongs to both plans and is excluded equally. Counting its interest cost in only one alternative would distort the comparison.

02

Give both alternatives the same starting money and outside budget

The example assigns CAD 5,000 of additional funds and CAD 16 of outside budget each month to either strategy. It uses a five-year horizon and an independently assumed 3% net effective annual alternative yield. These are authored inputs, not a current account offer.

Strategy A retains the CAD 5,000 in non-interest chequing. When a month qualifies for the waiver, its unused CAD 16 budget is deposited at month-end into a separate account earning the assumed yield. When a month does not qualify, that budget pays the fee.

Strategy B puts the same initial CAD 5,000 in the alternative account. Its CAD 16 outside budget pays the monthly fee every month. The model does not also remove that fee from B’s invested balance, because doing both would charge the same expense twice.

At the defaults, both strategies receive the same CAD 960 of outside budget over sixty months. A retains all of it as saving; B spends it on fees. If the household spends A’s freed budget instead, the resulting wealth path will differ from the saving behavior shown here.

03

Reconcile the ending resources instead of treating the waived fee as a yield

With all twelve months qualifying each year, A ends with approximately CAD 6,033.30: the unchanged CAD 5,000 plus saved fees and their growth. B ends with approximately CAD 5,796.37 from the same initial balance earning the assumed yield.

A therefore has about CAD 236.93 more ending resources under these conditions. The waterfall reconciles that difference. It adds CAD 960 of avoided fees actually saved, adds about CAD 73.30 of growth on those savings, then subtracts about CAD 796.37 of growth forgone on the additional balance.

The common CAD 5,000 cancels from the comparison. No fee principal or interest is counted twice. Neither endpoint includes the household’s other assets or any value assigned to account features.

FCAC’s account-maintenance fee review discusses both minimum-balance waivers and the opportunity cost of the funds retained. Its broader account-service comparison is a reason to check features separately, rather than conclude that a positive modeled difference identifies the best banking arrangement.

04

Use a break-even balance with a stated timing convention

The net effective annual yield is converted to an equivalent monthly rate: one plus the annual rate, raised to one-twelfth, minus one. Saved fees arrive at month-end and earn nothing before that month’s deposit.

With every month qualifying and a positive yield, the break-even additional balance equals the monthly fee divided by that monthly rate. At the default 3% net effective annual yield and CAD 16 monthly fee, it is approximately CAD 6,487.53.

This is an equal-ending-resources threshold under the selected saving behavior. It is not a required bank balance. Dividing an annual fee by an effective annual yield uses a different timing shortcut, so it need not give exactly the same result.

At a zero alternative yield, the model does not divide by zero. If any fee budget is saved, A has more resources for every finite extra balance in this limited comparison. If no fee saving exists either, all balances tie. Access, other charges and alternative uses outside this model still require their own assessment.

05

Stress eligibility and opportunity cost before changing accounts

The signed bars vary how many months qualify each year. The first listed months of each year qualify, and later months do not. This declared ordering matters because an earlier saved deposit has longer to earn the assumed yield.

The matrix changes the additional balance and net yield while retaining that same calendar and outside budget. Positive cells mean A ends with more modeled resources; negative cells mean B does. The cells carry no probability or promise that an account will waive its fee.

Before applying the comparison, review recent daily closing balances, upcoming bills and the actual waiver wording. Identify the extra cash that can remain assigned without being counted again as money for another goal.

Then compare transaction limits, service access, other fees, interest conditions and the reliability of the assumed alternative use. The extra balance remains the household’s money; the waiver condition does not make it legally inaccessible. Drawing on it may simply change eligibility. Keep that practical choice beside the numerical comparison.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All balances, fees, yields and qualifying months are original hypothetical inputs. The model compares equal starting funds and outside monthly budgets. It calculates neither a bank’s eligibility test nor a product recommendation; no observed fee or return dataset is encoded. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FCAC · Chequing accounts ↗

    Official HTML reviewed 25 October 2026 for fee waivers, balance conditions and the risk that a brief balance dip triggers a monthly fee. No named account, current fee quote, NSF rule or eligibility result is modeled.

    Official review dated 23 October 2026, checked 25 October 2026. Supports minimum-balance opportunity-cost and account-feature context. The charts use original assumptions and independent equal-resource arithmetic rather than the report’s product tables or numerical examples.
